newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania govt crackdown sparks opposition fury.
newsitem.headline: Albania govt crackdown sparks opposition fury.

text.p: The Albanian government carried out a wave of arrests across the country, in a move bitterly condemned by the main opposition Socialist Party, following widespread rioting.
The Interior Ministry said late on Wednesday it had detained numerous people in response to civil violence sparked by the dramatic collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid investment schemes.
The Socialists accused the ruling right-wing Democrats of intimidation and said they had imposed an effective state of emergency throughout the impoverished Balkan state.

A senior trade union leader earlier pledged to carry on peaceful protests until a comprehensive solution had been found to the investment fund scandal, which is believed to affect almost every Albanian.

A group of small right-wing parties called for a fresh anti-government protest in Tirana on Thursday while a coalition of opposition parties announced a demonstration in Albania's southernmost city, Gjirokaster.
Riots swept the country last weekend, with protesters setting fire to government buildings and offices of the Democratic Party in southern towns.

"In the districts where destruction and burning down of state institutions have taken place, the police have stopped and accompanied to the police stations a considerable number of citizens," the Interior Ministry said in a statement.
A ministry spokesman declined to say how many people had been arrested and said there was no political motivation behind the detentions.
The Socialist Party, reformed heirs of the old communist ruling class, said its leader in the southwestern city of Vlore had been arrested.
"Presently a de facto state of emergency has been established. Mass arrests have taken place," the secretary general of the Socialist Party, Rexhep Mejdani, told reporters.
"This shows the government tries to intimidate the population away from the peaceful process intended to solve its troubles."

Many Albanians plunged their life savings into a welter of pyramid schemes that flourished following the demise of the communist regime in late 1990. Critics blamed the government for the sudden collapse of some of the private schemes.
President Sali Berisha denied the charge but he indicated that people might not be fully compensated for any eventual pyramid losses.

Hours later police broke up an anti-government rally in Tirana organised by Azem Hajdari, the head of an independent trade union who was one of the leaders of the revolt which toppled the former communist elite.

Police swept demonstrators off the streets, punching and jostling people as they tried to reach the rally. Some camera crews and photographers said they were manhandled as police tried to prevent them from filming the scenes.

Parliament has given temporary powers to Berisha to use the army to maintain order. Taking no chances, the government has also cancelled all public sporting events this week to avoid large crowds gathering.
